messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was thirty-two when he came to the clinic, a park ranger with eight years of service in the Rocky Mountain region, though he hadn't worked in the field for the past eighteen months. He sat with his hands folded, shoulders drawn inward, and spoke in a measured voice that seemed to cost him effort. Three years ago, while on a solo patrol in a remote canyon, he had been ambushed and held captive for six days by a man fleeing federal custody. The man had restrained him, beaten him, and subjected him to repeated threats and degradation—the specific methods remained fragmented in Marcus's mind, some moments crystalline and horrifying, others dissolved into blank stretches he could not access or describe. He had been rescued when a search team finally located him, but rescue had not brought relief.

In the months after, Marcus had begun to notice his body's strange autonomy. His heart would race at the sound of footsteps behind him before his conscious mind registered anything threatening. His hands trembled when doors closed. He had come to believe that his nervous system had been permanently rewired by the ordeal—that whatever damage the man had inflicted was not just psychological but physiological, written into his body in ways he could not undo. This conviction shaped everything that followed. If his body was broken, if it could betray him by panicking at shadows, then the world itself must be far more dangerous than other people understood. He began checking the locks on his cabin obsessively, sometimes five or six times before bed, each check driven by a creeping certainty that danger was imminent, that his compromised body would not warn him in time. When his supervisor asked him to return to field work, Marcus felt the familiar surge of dread—not just fear of the wilderness, but a deeper conviction that he could no longer trust his own physical responses to keep him safe.

Unable to rely on his body, Marcus reasoned, he could at least control his mind. Before any interaction—a phone call to his sister, a conversation with a coworker, even a brief exchange with a cashier—he would rehearse what he might say, anticipating questions and preparing responses. The rehearsal gave him a thin sense of mastery, though it left him exhausted and sometimes unable to follow the actual conversation when it unfolded differently than he had scripted. When people asked him directly about what had happened, he would begin to explain and then lose the thread entirely, the narrative dissolving into fragments he could not sequence or articulate. Some moments remained brutally vivid—the cold of the restraints, the particular timbre of the man's voice—while others had vanished completely, leaving gaps he could not fill. The blanks terrified him more than the clarity did. He had come to fear that his inability to construct a coherent account of the trauma meant something was fundamentally wrong with him, that his mind was fracturing, that he was going crazy.

This fear fed his hypervigilance. When anything took longer than expected—a delayed email response, a friend taking longer to answer his call—Marcus's mind immediately conjured catastrophe. Something bad was happening. Someone was in danger. He was in danger. His body would tense, his breathing shallow, before he could even articulate what he feared. The more he tried to suppress these reactions, the more they seemed to confirm his deepest conviction: that he could not rely on other people to understand or protect him, that he had to manage everything himself. He had stopped accepting rides from colleagues and now drove himself everywhere, though driving triggered his body's alarm response so intensely that he often pulled over, gripping the steering wheel, unable to continue. He had begun numbing himself to his emotions, a kind of deliberate blankness he cultivated by refusing to think about his feelings or acknowledge them when they surfaced. This numbness made the hypervigilance worse, because without the grounding of his own emotional awareness, every external stimulus felt like a threat he had to monitor and control.

By the time Marcus sought help, he had withdrawn almost entirely from his life. He worked dispatch from an office, avoiding the field. He had not seen friends in months. His sister had stopped calling after he rehearsed their conversations so extensively that he could barely respond authentically to anything she said. What frightened him most was the thought that the damage was permanent, that he would spend the rest of his life trapped in this cycle of hypervigilance and numbness, unable to trust his body or his mind, unable to explain to anyone what had happened or why he could not seem to move forward.
